## Hands-on 4 – Exploring the menu {#hands-on-4-work-the-menu .smaller}

::: {.small}
**Task 4 is exploratory.** Try several specifications, look at what each one does, and get a feel for which decisions move the estimate.

1. Start from the reproduced specification, the model of C6HJR, which every argument of `try_spec()` takes as its default
2. Change **one decision** in `try_spec()` and read what happens to *b*, the partial *r*, the CR2 p and the placement; `my_experiments()` lists every try
3. Do it again with a different decision. Three or four is plenty, and one option that is off the curve, to read why it is refused
4. Then rerun the one you can argue for best with `try_spec()`, so that it is your last try, and **submit it** with `submit_exploration()`
:::

::: {.fs-80}
**In the IDE workspace:** Task 4 of `index.qmd`, from the chunk `try-baseline` to the chunk `submit-exploration`, or the section on Task 4 of `working_script.R`.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Your dot appears on the live **Class results** page within seconds. This is **not** your preregistered analysis: you are allowed to look, change your mind and try again, which is why this phase has a name of its own.
:::

::: notes
Task 4 is exploration, which differs from the preregistered analysis that comes later. Start from the reproduced specification, my own model, which every argument of `try_spec()` takes as its default, whichever analyst you reproduced. Change one decision, read what happens to the coefficient, the partial r, the CR2 p-value and the placement among the eight hundred and sixty-four, and then do it again with a different decision. Ask for one option off the curve as well and read the reason that comes back, then rerun the try for which you can argue best and submit it. On the next slides I run each step in the browser. [advance] Here, unlike in the preregistration, you are allowed to look, change your mind and try again.
:::

## Hands-on 4 – The reproduced specification {#hands-on-4-the-reproduced-specification .smaller}

::: {.small}
`try_spec()` with no arguments is the reproduced specification, the model of C6HJR, and every argument defaults to it. Read *b*, the claim-aligned partial *r*, the CR2 p and the placement among the `r format(nrow(spec_curve), big.mark = ",")`, the lines that every try prints.
:::

::: {.fs-80}
**In the IDE workspace:** the chunk `try-baseline` of `index.qmd`, where each call fits the model on your machine.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# The reproduced specification, the model of C6HJR in Task 3
try_spec()
```

::: notes
Every try starts from the reproduced specification. The cell calls `try_spec()` with no arguments, which gives my own model, since every argument defaults to it, so that changing one thing means changing one argument. [run it] The printout gives the slope with its conventional standard error and t, the claim-aligned partial r, the p-value of the test that classes every point of the curve, the class of the result and its placement among the eight hundred and sixty-four. The test clusters the errors by country with the CR2 correction, on nine point eight Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, and under it this specification is not significant at five per cent, with a p of point zero five zero four. In the slides the result is read from the curve that loaded with the data, while in your IDE workspace `try_spec()` fits the model and gives the same numbers.
:::

## Hands-on 4 – The question {#hands-on-4-the-question .smaller .output-8}

::: {.fs-80}
Each cell changes one decision and holds the others; the first four change the question, here the outcome scale and the estimator.\
**In the IDE workspace:** the chunk `try-one-at-a-time` of `index.qmd`, whose six calls are the cells of this slide and the next two.
:::

::: {.fs-80}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(outcome = "mpos")  # the composite of both positive framings
```
:::

::: {.fs-80}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(estimator = "fe_country")  # country effects only: changes common to all of Europe stay in
```
:::

::: notes
One decision changes at a time and the others are held, so that when a number moves you can say what moved it. The first four calls change the question asked of the data. The first replaces the cosmopolitan scale by the composite of both positive framings, and the second keeps the country effects and drops the year effects, so that the changes that every country went through in the same year stay in the comparison. [run both] On the composite the claim-aligned r goes from minus point two four to minus point three one, and the CR2 p falls below five per cent; without the year effects it goes to minus point four. In your report the six calls of this slide and the next two sit in one chunk, `try-one-at-a-time`.
:::

## Hands-on 4 – The question, continued {#hands-on-4-the-question-continued .smaller .output-8}

::: {.fs-80}
GDP growth in place of unemployment, with the signs flipped so that below zero stays the direction of the claim, and growth held fixed beside unemployment.\
**In the IDE workspace:** the chunk `try-one-at-a-time` of `index.qmd`.
:::

::: {.fs-80}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(predictor = "growth")  # GDP growth instead of unemployment, in the World Bank series
```
:::

::: {.fs-80}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(copredictor = "other")  # adjusted for the other economic measure, here GDP growth
```
:::

::: notes
The next two calls change the measure of the economy. The first measures it by GDP growth in the World Bank series instead of unemployment, and because the claim expects framing to rise with growth, the printout reverses the signs, so that below zero stays the direction of the claim. The second keeps unemployment and adjusts for growth, the co-predictor of the menu, which is the arrow of Hands-on 2 that fixed effects cannot reach. [run both] On growth alone the claim-aligned r shrinks to minus point zero seven and is far from significant. With growth held fixed, unemployment keeps almost all of its estimate, at minus point two three, and its CR2 p falls to point zero two seven.
:::

## Hands-on 4 – Measurement {#hands-on-4-measurement .smaller .output-8}

::: {.fs-80}
The same question, measured otherwise: the respondents who mentioned no frame left out instead of scored zero, and a Eurostat series of unemployment.\
**In the IDE workspace:** the chunk `try-one-at-a-time` of `index.qmd`.
:::

::: {.fs-80}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(noop = "drop")  # leave out the respondents who mentioned no frame
```
:::

::: {.fs-80}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
try_spec(measure = "es_2064_pop")  # a Eurostat unemployment series instead of the World Bank one
```
:::

::: notes
The last two calls keep the question and change only how it is measured. The first leaves out the respondents who mentioned no frame at all, whom the reproduced specification scores zero, and the second replaces the World Bank series of unemployment with a Eurostat series, the unemployed as a share of the whole population aged twenty to sixty-four, the definition used by KQXUE. [run both] Leaving the silent respondents out moves the claim-aligned r to minus point three one, with a CR2 p of point zero one three, and the Eurostat series moves it to minus point two three, with a p just under point zero seven. These measurement decisions move the estimate less than the estimator does, but they can move the test across the line.
:::

## Hands-on 4 – Options off the curve {#hands-on-4-options-off-the-curve .smaller}

::: {.small}
The menu holds more options than the curve, which keeps only the options that answer this claim in a justifiable way. Ask for another, and the helper refuses it, gives the reason and names the workshop's page that teaches it. Edit the cell to try `sample = "no_bailout"`, `weights = "pop"`, `construction = "count"`, `family = "beta"` or `outcome = "mneg"`.
:::

::: {.fs-80}
**In the IDE workspace:** the chunk `try-off-curve` of `index.qmd`, marked `error: true` so that the refusal does not stop the render.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# An option that is not on the curve: the helper refuses it and says why.
try_spec(estimator = "pooled_cl")
```

::: notes
The curve keeps only the options that answer this claim in a justifiable way, and every other option of the menu is still an argument of `try_spec()`. This cell asks for pooled OLS, the estimator with no fixed effects at all. [run it] The helper refuses it, and prints the reason why the option is not on the curve, the page of the workshop's website that teaches it, and the options that stay on the curve. Edit the cell for another option, such as a sample without the bailout countries, a weight by population or a negative scale, and read each reason. In your report the chunk `try-off-curve` makes the same request, marked so that the refusal does not stop the render.
:::

## Hands-on 4 – Every argument {#hands-on-4-every-argument .smaller .output-8}

::: {.fs-80}
The full set of arguments, each with the reproduced specification as its default and the options of the menu in the comment beside it.\
**In the IDE workspace:** calls of your own, written after the chunk `try-off-curve` of `index.qmd` or in the console.
:::

::: {.fs-70}
```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| max-lines: 12
try_spec(
  # The question
  outcome      = "mcosmo",       # mcosmo | mutil | mpos          off the curve: mcomm | mlib | mneg
  predictor    = "unemp",        # unemp | growth
  copredictor  = "none",         # none | other   (the other economic measure, adjusted for)
  estimator    = "fe_twoway",    # fe_twoway | fe_country         off the curve: re | pooled_cl
  sample       = "all",          # all       off the curve: y2004_2008 | y2009_2013 | no_bailout | no_GR_ES
  weights      = "none",         # none      off the curve: n_cell | n_eff | pop
  construction = "share",        # share     off the curve: count | rate
  # Measurement
  noop         = "zero",         # zero | drop                    off the curve: split | mi_mice | mi_amelia
  item_set     = "all",          # all | un   (with or without the "unemployment" item)
  cell_weight  = "unweighted",   # unweighted | design
  measure      = "wb_nat",       # unemp:  wb_nat | es_1574_act | es_2064_pop | es_2564_lfs   off: es_1574_tips
                                 # growth: wb_growth                                          off: es_growth
  # The model
  pred_form    = "raw",          # raw | log   (growth: raw only)
  family       = "gaussian",     # gaussian  off the curve: beta
  se           = "cr2"           # cr2, fixed: CR2 errors clustered by country test every result
)
```
:::

::: notes
This call holds the full set of arguments, each with the reproduced specification as its default and the options of the menu in the comment beside it, in the three groups of the menu, the question, measurement and the model. It is the cell to edit when you design a try of your own: change two or three lines and run it, and the printout has the same lines as before. [run it] The last argument, the inference rule, is fixed, since every result on the curve is tested by CR2 errors clustered by country. In your IDE workspace you write such calls yourself, after the chunk of the refused option or in the console, and each one fits the model on your machine.
:::

## Hands-on 4 – The submission {#hands-on-4-the-submission .smaller .output-8}

::: {.fs-80}
`my_experiments()` lists every try; rerun the one that you would defend and **submit it**: the cell prints your tag, such as `amber-otter-42`, and the link to the form, and your dot joins the [Class results]({{< var live-results-url >}}) page.\
**In the IDE workspace:** the chunks `my-experiments` and `submit-exploration` of `index.qmd`, with the tag in the file `.class-tag`.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
my_experiments()
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
submit_exploration()
```

::: notes
When you have three or four tries, print the log. `my_experiments()` lists the tries side by side, showing only the decisions that you varied, which makes up the small multiverse that you have just built. Then rerun the try for which you can argue best, so that it is your last, and submit it. [run both] The cell prints your submission line, a link to a form with every field filled in, and a tag that marks your dot on the class chart. Press Send in the form, and the dot appears on the Class results page within seconds, labelled exploratory because you chose it after looking at the results. In your IDE workspace the tag is kept in a file, so that both of your submissions carry it. [keep the Class results page on the shared screen and press Run Code as the dots land]
:::
